originalTitle: Disruption review – anti-AI thriller boasts knockout cast but tech commentary needs an update
summary: John David Washington leads an exceptionally talented cast in a sleek off-Broadway thriller that feels a little dated
content: Making its US debut three years after its London premiere, Andrew Stein’s Disruption faces the typical battle of the topical play: even with the most expedient fast-track to production, works tackling current events are in danger of obsolescence upon arrival, often left at the mercy of the latest update, for better or worse. As far as plays dealing with AI go, New York got Ayad Akhtar’s McNeal in 2024, which condescended while saying next to nothing about ChatGPT plagiarism, and was marred, for me, by news of star Robert Downey Jr’s $100m Avengers payday. And earlier this year, the tech-industry moral quandary of Matthew Libby’s Data received bone-chilling boosts from unfolding reports of Palantir’s work with ICE. Stein’s play has to do with the vast amounts of personal information we freely hand over to our tech overlords, and how it could be leveraged against us. It is well-constructed, briskly directed by Hersh Ellis, and with handsome scenic and costume designs by Zoë Hurwitz – both of whom also worked on its 2023 iteration. But aside from a late development that echoes last week’s jump-scare that an OpenAI tool went rogue, any insights it offers about our present moment are either naively outdated or mired in its overcomplicated web of characters. Charitably, one could chalk this up to the three years lapsed since its premiere; 30 lifetimes in cyberland. But lines like “Data’s the next frontier,” or “Technology has made us so connected to everything except ourselves,” would not have stood a chance in 2010. What this Off-Broadway production has best going for it is an absurdly talented cast representing some of the city’s best and most versatile actors. They’re paired off in appealing ways and it’s quite fun, to reference another archaic technology, to watch them bounce off each other like a DVD screensaver. Stein efficiently sketches their milieu and subtle differences as they prepare for a night out: Ben (Conrad Ricamora) and Suzie (Shaunette Renée Wilson) are a chic, uptown match, debating whether to vacation in Machu Picchu or the Galápagos; Mia (Irene Sofia Lucio) and surgeon Barry (Jason Ralph) wear athleisure and live in Brooklyn, but are regretful they passed on a $3m brownstone; and on-the-rocks Jill (Elizabeth Stanley) and Paul (Joe Tippett) stress over whether they can make the last train home to Westchester. All are in their late 30s, early 40s, and don’t seem to like each other very much any more, but are gathered for dinner by their old friend Nick (John David Washington), a mega-successful entrepreneur, in town from San Francisco with a business proposal and a mysterious younger colleague, Raven (Emma Kikue). Why the wives all come in resisting Nick’s plan, which he’d intimated in advance, is never really defined, but they successfully (for now) prevent their husbands from investing in his venture, which Nick terms “Waze, but for your life” – an AI-driven algorithm to assist with any and all life decisions. ChatGPT has come a long way since the play’s inception, and the fact that Nick’s idea is no longer novel could be forgiven had the play explored it more thoroughly. Instead of leading his characters into some version of AI psychosis, though, Stein pivots to a sort of blackmail plot that is compelling in its own right, but whose late arrival jerks the concept in a different direction. The idea is that the secrets to which our smart devices are privy could readily be weaponized, but it jostles for air with the tangle (and, it turns out, incestuousness) of this octet’s dynamics. I admire a production like Disruption, which hands a top-notch cast adult, contemporary material. (Any chance to watch Elizabeth Stanley flex her comedic muscle is a boon.) Rushing to meet headlines might always yield hasty results, but at least we can be grateful that, in its messiness, Stein seems defiantly anti-AI.
chineseTitle: 颠覆评论——反 AI 惊悚片拥有出色的演员阵容，但技术评论需要更新
chineseSummary: 约翰·大卫·华盛顿在这部时尚的非百老汇惊悚片中领衔才华横溢的演员阵容，但感觉有点过时了
chineseContent: 安德鲁·斯坦的《颠覆》在伦敦首映三年后在美国首演，面临着典型的话题剧之战：即使有最便捷的快速制作，处理时事的作品在抵达后也面临着过时的危险，往往会受到最新更新的摆布，无论好坏。就涉及人工智能的戏剧而言，纽约在 2024 年迎来了阿亚德·阿赫塔尔 (Ayad Akhtar) 饰演的麦克尼尔 (McNeal)，该剧居高临下，几乎没有提及 ChatGPT 的抄袭行为，而对我来说，明星小罗伯特·唐尼 (Robert Downey Jr) 获得 1 亿美元《复仇者联盟》片酬的消息也让我感到受损。今年早些时候，Palantir 与 ICE 合作的报道进一步加剧了 Matthew Libby 数据中的科技行业道德困境。斯坦因的游戏与我们自由地交给我们的科技霸主的大量个人信息以及如何利用这些信息来对付我们有关。该片结构精良，导演赫什·埃利斯 (Hersh Ellis) 轻快，佐伊·赫尔维茨 (Zoë Hurwitz) 设计了漂亮的布景和服装——两人也参与了 2023 年版本的制作。但除了与上周 OpenAI 工具失控的恐慌相呼应的最新进展之外，它提供的有关我们当前时刻的任何见解要么天真地过时，要么陷入其过于复杂的字符网络中。仁慈地说，人们可以把这归因于自首映以来已经过去了三年；赛博世界 30 辈子。但像“数据是下一个前沿”或“技术让我们与除了我们自己之外的一切事物都紧密相连”这样的台词在 2010 年就没有机会出现了。这部非百老汇作品的最大优点是拥有一群才华横溢的演员阵容，他们代表了这座城市最优秀、最多才多艺的演员。它们以吸引人的方式配对，参考另一种古老的技术，看它们如何搭配，这很有趣。
whyItMatters: 这条信息属于全球新闻信号，适合用于观察外部环境、政策变化、地缘风险和市场情绪。
